questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to study in an Asian country since I have never been in Asia before.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Best time of my life so far.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: The University of Tokyo provides a comprehensive program timeline and to-do list that covers everything important for the exchange. This includes everything university related and also mandatory administrative procedures (residence registration, health care etc.). It's an easy to find and easy to understand google site that is continuously updated with relevant information.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There was a mandatory orientation day where the most important information was covered. We were then grouped with other people from the exchange program (ca. 8 people) and UTokyo students (1-2 people). The UTokyo students showed us the campus and we could ask them questions about campus life, life in Japan or whatever interested us. They would also organize social events with the group like day-trips to places around Tokyo,  watching fireworks, dinners, visiting temples etc. throughout the whole duration of the semester.

How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: The Komaba Lodge is only 5 minutes walking from the Komaba campus. In my view, it is the best option if most of your classes are on the Komaba campus. It is also extremely close to Shibuya which means you live next to one of the most vibrant areas in Tokyo and you can get everywhere rather quickly. There is also the Mejirodai International Village, which is closer to the Hongo campus. So if you plan to have a lot of courses in Hongo it might be the smarter choice. However, me and many other people also had classes in Hongo while living in the Komaba Lodge and commuting was no problem. I would even go so far and say that commuting from Komaba Lodge to Hongo Campus (it takes approx. 45-60mins) helped me to navigate the city better and get used to Tokyo's busy public transportation.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: In the Komaba Lodge we had a shared kitchen for each floor. You share it with about 30 people. It is frankly not the most modern kitchen but it works and you have plenty of space. Since eating outside is generally cheaper than cooking, I never really used the kitchen, except when I made breakfast or for social gatherings.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: I think Komaba Lodge was by far the best choice. Mostly because it is exceptionally located and convenient – may it be that you like to wake up 10 minutes before class starts or if you love to spend long nights out without being stranded. You pay a little bit more rent compared to the other dorms but you have your own bathroom, which was a huge plus for me. Your social life will most likely be built around your dorm as well and I have made some great friends in there. Living on campus is definitely the most uncomplicated and fun way to live during your exchange.

How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: If you are a USTEP student, you search for courses you are eligible to take in the online course catalogue. Make sure you meet the language requirements if you want to take a course that is taught in Japanese. You must enroll in a minimum of 6 periods per week, which is very manageable. This means, even if KU requires you to only do 4 courses, for example, you still need to do 2 extra courses as required by UTokyo. You register your classes in the first weeks of the semester on UTAS and afterwards you use UTOL for class instructions etc.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The University of Tokyo provides very clear instructions on how to register courses. You will find them in the aforementioned program timeline and to-do list.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was able to register every class that was pre-approved without any issues. I also tried to take a Japanese-language course but my level was too low to attend the Japanese-language beginners course. That confused me a bit. However, I could still do a non-credit Japanese-language course. Additionally, there are some popular classes with limited capacity (mostly film or photography related courses). You don't necessarily have to register them as fast as possible but it's very likely that they will be overfilled. The instructor will then either raffle or filter out by conducting a survey which you have to fill out in time.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: If possible, try out new scientific fields you were always curious about. Also, the seemingly non-challenging courses about film etc. can be way more time-consuming and demanding than anticipated.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The course catalogue for exchange students is large but could still be expanded, especially when it comes to courses that are taught in English.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: In my view, the courses were not as demanding as courses at KU. It shouldn't be an issue to achieve a passing grade. However, some classes bind grades to attendance, so sometimes you have to be careful not to miss any classes without a valid reason.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The teaching style was quite similar. However, my courses consisted mostly of seminars, instead of larger lectures. For some classes we only had about 4-10 students which made it way more personal and interactive.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Nothing really unexpected but if you plan to travel around Tokyo and Japan, you will obviously face higher monthly transportation costs.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Groceries, especially fresh fruit and vegetables were more expensive than I expected. On the other side, you can get meals in the canteen for very cheap if you get a COOP member card. Also a lot of places (museums, tourist attractions, parks etc.) have a student discount, so it never hurts to ask :)

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: UTokyo has clubs and circles for nearly everything. Clubs are intensive and competitive while circles are more recreational – just keep that in mind. You can do all kinds of sports (e.g., football, volleyball, baseball, karate, archery etc.), cultural activities (e.g., japanese traditional music, tea ceremonies, art) and countless more social activities (e.g., poker, debating, model trains, beyblades, shooting or airplane flying). Just check out UT-Base online or look out for the wooden signs that are prominently displayed around campus to find your favorite clubs and circles.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I can recommend joining at least one circle in order to have the full campus-life experience. Whatever you want to do, there will definitely be a club or circle for it. It is a good way to connect with local students. But it might be hard to join some circles if you don't speak Japanese.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: If you have the financial resources, you should definitely travel around Japan or even neighboring countries (China, Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam). Public transportation allows you to travel long distances cheaply and swiftly. There are a lot of beautiful places close by such as Nikko, Yokohama, Kamakura or Fuji. Tokyo is also such a vast city, so if you have time you should explore it as much as you can. You will always find something new and exciting. But of course, you shouldn't miss other bigger cities like Osaka, Kyoto or Hiroshima as well.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Relatively easy, although it may take some time. You can always look up the do's and don'ts online or ask a person from Japan about proper social etiquettes. The rest is just exposure therapy.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Socializing with local UTokyo students might be easiest if you can conversate in Japanese. Unfortunately, most Japanese students do not speak English on a level that is comparable to Danish or European standards. Nevertheless, you can still make friends with UTokyo students as I believe most people are good-willing and kind. Sometimes, you may find yourself be approached by curious students on campus, other times it doesn't hurt to make the first step yourself. A great way to organically meet local students is through clubs and circles.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The language barrier was stronger than I anticipated. Many people do not really speak English (fluently), so you might get into situations where you have to completely rely on a translation tool. Yet, people seem to appreciate it when you at least try to speak Japanese. I can recommend learning some essential Japanese phrases as preparation.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The food culture. You can find affordable restaurants with delicious meals everywhere, around the clock. I loved going out every day to eat and drink together with friends. It was something I could not afford doing as a student in Europe, especially Denmark.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Join a circle or club. Get the COOP member card for cheaper canteen meals. Travel around Japan as much as you can.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: If you want to impress random Japanese people, you can just tell them that you study at "Todai".

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Attending courses in academic fields I could not take previously as part of my studies and making new friends from many parts of the world.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Saying goodbye.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: I would go on exchange in Tokyo again if I could.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
